title: Psalm 43: Send Out Your Light and Your Truth
summary: A worshiper far from the temple asks God to take up his case against deceitful and unjust people. He cannot understand why God seems to have rejected him, and he asks for God's light and truth to lead him back to the holy mountain and the altar. The psalm closes with the same refrain that runs through Psalm 42: a man talking to his own downcast soul and telling it to hope in God.
story: Psalm 43 is the last movement of a single song that begins in Psalm 42, the opening psalm of Book II of the Psalter (Psalms 42 to 72). In Psalm 42 a man who once led crowds to the house of God is now cut off from it, taunted by people who ask where his God is. Psalm 43 carries that grief one step further. The complaint is the same, but for the first time the singer asks for something concrete: to be led home. It is the turn from remembering worship to praying for it again, and it closes the first Korahite group with a hope that has not yet been answered but has begun to look forward.
historical:
Psalm 43 has no heading, which is unusual in Book II, where nearly every psalm carries one. That absence, together with the shared refrain (Psalm 42:5, 42:11, and 43:5) and the shared vocabulary of mourning and oppression by the enemy, has led most interpreters to treat Psalms 42 and 43 as one poem later divided. A number of Hebrew manuscripts copy them as a single psalm. If so, the heading of Psalm 42 covers this one too: a Maskil of the sons of Korah, one of the Levite families of temple singers.

The setting can only be inferred. Psalm 42 places the speaker in the far north, near the Jordan's sources and Mount Hermon, and here he pleads against an ungodly nation. Some have proposed a Levite carried off in an invasion or exiled after Jerusalem's fall in 587 or 586 BC; others think of someone kept from Jerusalem by illness or circumstance in the monarchy period. The text names no event, and the psalm has been prayed ever since by people who cannot reach the place where they used to meet God.
cultural:
The request to be brought to God's holy mountain and to the place where he dwells refers to Mount Zion and the temple in Jerusalem, where Israel believed God had set his name and where sacrifices were offered at the altar. For an Israelite, going up to the temple at the great festivals was a central act of faith. Being unable to go was not a small inconvenience; it felt like being cut off from God's presence itself.

The lyre (kinnor), mentioned in verse 4, was the common stringed instrument of Israelite worship, the instrument David played for Saul. The singer imagines himself back among the temple musicians. The opening words, a plea for God to vindicate and plead his case, come from the law court: the psalmist asks God to act as his advocate and judge against people who have lied about him.
literary: The psalm is an individual lament, the most common type in the Psalter: an address to God, a complaint, a request, and an expression of trust. Verse 1 is the petition, verse 2 the complaint (with the two questions "Why have You rejected me?" and "Why must I walk in sorrow"), verses 3 and 4 the request and vow, and verse 5 the refrain. Verse 2 almost repeats Psalm 42:9, but it swaps "forgotten" for "rejected", a sharper word. Light and truth in verse 3 are personified as God's messengers or guides, sent out to escort the singer home. The refrain in verse 5 is inward speech: the soul is addressed as though it were another person who needs to be reasoned with.

outline.t: A plea for justice and a question about rejection
Light and truth to lead the singer back to the altar

doctrines.note: The psalm shows that honest complaint and trust live side by side in prayer. The singer asks God why he has been rejected, and in the same breath calls him "the God of my refuge". Prayer here also includes speaking truth to one's own soul.
The refrain does not deny the sorrow; it looks past it. "I will yet praise Him" places joy in the future, grounded in who God is rather than in present feelings.
God's light and truth are not abstractions; they are sent to lead a person home to God's presence. Scripture regularly pictures God's word as light that guides the steps of the faithful.

words.note: Zanach, to reject or cast off. It is a strong word, used of God spurning his people or a king (Psalm 44:9 and 89:38 use it too). The singer feels discarded, not merely overlooked, and he says so to God directly.

Emet, truth, faithfulness, reliability. The word describes what can be leaned on without collapsing. Paired with light in verse 3, it names God's faithfulness as a guide that can be trusted when everything else, including the singer's own feelings, is unreliable.
Yachal, to wait or hope. In the Old Testament hope is less a feeling than a posture: waiting in expectation on someone who has promised. The refrain uses it as a command to one's own soul.

christ: The New Testament does not quote this psalm directly, and the connection to Christ is thematic. The request for God to send out his light and truth to lead a person into his presence finds its answer, for Christians, in Jesus, who calls himself the light of the world and the truth (John 8:12; 14:6) and who opens the way into God's presence. The downcast soul of the refrain also has an echo in Gethsemane, where Jesus says that his soul is very sorrowful, even to death, using language that recalls the Greek version of these Korahite psalms (Mark 14:34; Matthew 26:38). The one who leads people home himself knew the anguish of the psalmist.

hard.q: Why does a faithful person feel rejected by God, and is it wrong to say so?
hard.a: The psalmist doesn't claim to know why God seems absent. He calls God his refuge and, in the same verse, asks why God has rejected him. The Psalms treat this as a legitimate prayer, not a lapse of faith; laments make up a large portion of the Psalter. Some readers take such complaints as describing how things feel rather than how they are, and that is part of it. But the psalm does not correct the singer, and Scripture includes his words as prayers for others to use. The pattern the psalm offers is not suppression of the question but bringing it to God and pairing it with a stubborn decision to hope.

questions: The singer talks to his own soul in the refrain. What would you need to say to yourself in a season when God seems far away?
What does it mean to ask for God's light and truth to lead you, rather than simply to explain things to you?
Where do you go, or long to go, to meet God, and what happens to your faith when you can't get there?
